hints: Look for a carbon joined to four different groups in P, check the alpha carbon next to the ester group against the $CH_2$ and $OCH_3$ carbons.
walkthrough:
Recall what makes a carbon chiral**
Think of a carbon with four completely different arms. If you can swap any two arms and get a non superimposable mirror image, it is chiral. In P, $C_6H_5CH_2CH(NH_2)CO_2CH_3$, most carbons fail this test because they have at least two identical H atoms or are part of the planar ring.

Spot the only carbon with four different groups**
Focus on the carbon carrying $H_2N$. It is bonded to $H$, to $NH_2$, to $CH_2C_6H_5$ and to $CO_2CH_3$. All four are different, so mark this alpha carbon with * . No other carbon qualifies.
Final answer: Asterisk (*) on the alpha carbon, $C_6H_5CH_2CH^*(NH_2)CO_2CH_3$, the carbon bonded to $NH_2$.

hints: Recall what a polarimeter shows when plane polarised light passes through a single pure enantiomer.
Think how a pair of mirror image enantiomers compare in magnitude and direction of rotation.
walkthrough:
Picture what optical activity does**
Imagine plane polarised light as a wave vibrating in one plane. When it passes through a chiral sample, that plane twists by a characteristic angle. Because each sample here is a pure single enantiomer, each one will definitely show a rotation, that is the similarity.

Compare mirror images**
Now think of the two enantiomers as left and right hands. They interact with light in exactly opposite ways. So one will rotate light clockwise (+) and the other anticlockwise (-) by exactly the same number of degrees. Equal magnitude, opposite sign, that is the difference.

Final answer: Both pure enantiomers rotate the plane of plane polarised light.
Rotation is by the same angle but in opposite directions.

hints: Compare P ($NH_2$) with Q ($NHCOCH_3$) and identify what acyl fragment has been added to nitrogen.
walkthrough:
See the functional group change**
Look closely at nitrogen. In P it is a primary amine, $NH_2$. In Q it is $NHCOCH_3$, a secondary amide. So an ethanoyl group, $CH_3CO$, has been attached to N. That is acylation.

Choose the acylating agent**
The clean single step reagent for this is ethanoyl chloride, $CH_3COCl$. The $Cl$ leaves with the $H$ from the amine: $$C_6H_5CH_2CH(NH_2)CO_2CH_3 + CH_3COCl \rightarrow C_6H_5CH_2CH(NHCOCH_3)CO_2CH_3 + HCl$$ So the other product is hydrogen chloride, $HCl$.

Final answer: Compound added to P: $CH_3COCl$, ethanoyl chloride.
Other product: $HCl$.

hints: Recall the rule given: ester + $4[H]$ gives two alcohols, so split Q at the $CO_2CH_3$ group to find the methanol fragment.
Think what excess $LiAlH_4$ does to an amide carbonyl, $CH_3CONH$, when the $C=O$ becomes $CH_2$.
Check which part of Q is untouched by $LiAlH_4$, the benzene ring and the carbon skeleton $C_6H_5CH_2CH$.
walkthrough:
Split the ester first**
Take Q: $C_6H_5CH_2CH(NHCOCH_3)CO_2CH_3$. Reduction of the ester $CO_2CH_3$ with $LiAlH_4$ cleaves it into two alcohols. The $OCH_3$ side simply becomes $CH_3OH$, methanol. The acyl side becomes a primary alcohol, $CH_2OH$.

Reduce the amide to an amine**
Now look at the amide $NHCOCH_3$. With excess $LiAlH_4$, the $C=O$ is fully reduced to $CH_2$. So $NHCOCH_3$ becomes $NHCH_2CH_3$, a secondary amine with an ethyl group. This is why excess reagent matters, both carbonyls are attacked.

Assemble the second organic product**
Keep the untouched backbone $C_6H_5CH_2CH$ together. Attach the new $NHCH_2CH_3$ and the new $CH_2OH$: $$C_6H_5CH_2CH(NHCOCH_3)CO_2CH_3 + [H] \rightarrow C_6H_5CH_2CH(NHCH_2CH_3)CH_2OH + CH_3OH$$ The benzene ring does not react with $LiAlH_4$.

Final answer: Product 1: methanol, $CH_3OH$.
Product 2: $C_6H_5CH_2CH(NHCH_2CH_3)CH_2OH$, 2-(ethylamino)-3-phenylpropan-1-ol. Ester reduced to primary alcohol, amide reduced to secondary amine, benzene ring unchanged.

hints: Rank the nitrogen types first: alkyl amine in P, aromatic amine in phenylamine, amide in Q, and recall basicity means availability of the lone pair to accept $H^+$.
Consider why the lone pair on phenylamine is less available due to overlap with the benzene pi system.
Compare the alkyl group in P with the $C=O$ group in Q and how they push or pull electron density away from nitrogen.
walkthrough:
Define basicity at nitrogen**
Think like a proton. A base is a lone pair donor. The more electron rich and free the lone pair on N is, the stronger the base. So ask for each compound: how free is the lone pair to grab $H^+$?

Place P at the top**
P has an aliphatic primary amine, $RNH_2$. The alkyl group pushes electrons toward N by a positive inductive effect. That increases electron density on N and makes the lone pair very available. So P is the most basic.

Place phenylamine in the middle**
In phenylamine, $C_6H_5NH_2$, the lone pair on N can overlap with the pi cloud of the ring. The p-orbital on N overlaps with the ring, delocalising the lone pair into the ring and lowering electron density on N. It is still more available than an amide, but much less than P.

Place Q at the bottom**
Q has an amide, $RNHCOR$. Here the lone pair on N overlaps strongly with the adjacent $C=O$. Delocalisation of the N lone pair onto oxygen leaves N electron poor and hardly able to accept $H^+$. So Q is the least basic. Overall: $$Q < phenylamine < P$$

Final answer: Q < phenylamine < P (least basic to most basic).
Basicity depends on availability of N lone pair to accept a proton.
In phenylamine the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring by overlap of N p-orbital with ring pi system, less available.
In P the alkyl group has positive inductive effect, increasing electron density on N, most available.
In Q the N lone pair is delocalised into the $C=O$ group, least available.

hints: Look at Fig. 7.2: the ring gains a para $NH_2$ group and the methyl ester becomes a carboxylic acid, so one step must nitrate the ring.
Recall the two stage route from $NO_2$ to $NH_2$ using tin and concentrated acid, and that nitration needs conc. acids.
walkthrough:
Plan the ring transformation**
Compare P and R. The side chain $CH(NH_2)CO_2CH_3$ becomes $CH(NH_2)CO_2H$, so the ester is hydrolysed to acid. More importantly, the benzene gains a para $NH_2$. The standard way to put $NH_2$ on a ring is to nitrate then reduce. So step 1 is nitration with concentrated $HNO_3$ and concentrated $H_2SO_4$ at about $25$ to $60^{\circ}C$.

Reduce nitro to amine**
The nitro intermediate, $C_6H_4(NO_2)CH_2CH(NH_2)CO_2H$, must be reduced. Use $Sn$ and concentrated $HCl$ heated under reflux, then neutralise with $NaOH(aq)$ to liberate the free amine. That gives the para $H_2N-C_6H_4$ group in R.

Final answer: Step 1: conc. $HNO_3$ and conc. $H_2SO_4$, $25^{\circ}C < T \leq 60^{\circ}C$ (nitration, also hydrolyses ester under acidic conditions or separate acid hydrolysis).
Step 2: $Sn$ and conc. $HCl$ with reflux, followed by $NaOH(aq)$ (reduction of $NO_2$ to $NH_2$).

hints: Recall what cold $HNO_2$ does to a primary aromatic amine at $4^{\circ}C$.
Recall where bromine substitutes on a strongly activating $NH_2$ ring with excess $Br_2(aq)$.
walkthrough:
Form the diazonium ion**
R has two $NH_2$ groups, but only the aromatic one diazotises. Cold nitrous acid, $HNO_2$ at $4^{\circ}C$, converts $Ar-NH_2$ into $Ar-N_2^+$. So draw R unchanged except the para $NH_2$ on the ring becomes $N_2^+$. The aliphatic $H_2NCH$ and $CO_2H$ stay intact.

Brominate the activated ring**
The $H_2N$ ring is hugely activated toward electrophilic substitution. Excess $Br_2(aq)$ at room temperature gives 2,6-dibromination, that is both ortho positions to the aromatic $NH_2$. The side chain $H_2NCH(CH_2)CO_2H$ is unchanged. So the product keeps the aromatic $NH_2$ with two $Br$ atoms flanking it.

Final answer: With $HNO_2(aq)$ at $4^{\circ}C$: diazonium salt, $H_2NCH(CH_2C_6H_4N_2^+\,para)CO_2H$ (aromatic $NH_2$ becomes $N_2^+$).
With excess $Br_2(aq)$: dibromo product, $H_2NCH(CH_2C_6H_2Br_2NH_2)CO_2H$ with two $Br$ at 2,6 positions ortho to the aromatic $NH_2$.

hints: Think of T as an amino acid that can exist as cation, zwitterion and anion depending on pH.
walkthrough:
Link pH to charge**
Picture T, phenylalanine $C_6H_5CH_2CH(NH_2)CO_2H$, in water. At low pH both groups are protonated ($NH_3^+$, $CO_2H$). At high pH both are deprotonated ($NH_2$, $CO_2^-$). In the middle it exists as $NH_3^+$ and $CO_2^-$ together, a zwitterion with zero net charge.

Define the special pH**
The isoelectric point is exactly that middle pH where the neutral zwitterion dominates and the average charge is zero.
Final answer: The pH at which the zwitterion is the dominant form, where the species is electrically neutral overall.

hints: Recall that an amino acid with $NH_2$ and $CO_2H$ polymerises by forming amide (peptide) links with loss of water.
Draw three T units joined $CO$ to $NH$ in a chain and clearly label the repeat unit with brackets.
walkthrough:
Make the peptide link**
Line up the $CO_2H$ of one T with the $H_2N$ of the next. Water is lost and a $CONH$ amide link forms: $$RCO_2H + H_2NR' \rightarrow RCONHR' + H_2O$$ Repeat this to join three monomers head to tail.

Show three units and mark the repeat**
Draw $NHCH(CH_2C_6H_5)CO$ repeated three times in a continuous chain, with all $CH(CH_2C_6H_5)$ groups correct and free bonds at the ends shown. Put brackets around one $NHCH(CH_2C_6H_5)CO$ unit and label it repeat unit.

Final answer: Section with three T monomers joined by amide / peptide links: $-[NHCH(CH_2C_6H_5)CO]-[NHCH(CH_2C_6H_5)CO]-[NHCH(CH_2C_6H_5)CO]-$ with correct trailing bonds and repeat unit identified by brackets / label.
